explanations.explanation: Son, friend. The writer says Abraham was ready to offer his one and only son on the altar. This is the man who had received the promises, so the stakes couldn't be higher. I think this one hurts, so I'll say it once and let it sit.
Abraham was the one being tested here. The verse says he was ready to offer his one and only son, not a lamb. That son was Isaac, and I think that's what makes this verse so heavy.
The verse doesn't say servant, friend. Abraham was ready to offer his one and only son. God had said, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” That's why this test weighs so much.

explanations.answer: He reasoned that God could raise the dead
explanations.explanation: That's how Abraham held it together, friend. The promise says Isaac and the test says Isaac, and he lands on this: “Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead…” The writer adds that in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.

explanations.answer: He figured God would change His mind
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different answer. It says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead. God's words were “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” Nothing in these verses says Abraham expected God to change course.

explanations.answer: He decided the promise meant someone else
explanations.explanation: The promise names Isaac, friend: “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” The verse never says Abraham read it as someone else. What it says is that Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead. So he kept the promise and the test side by side.

True, friend. The writer says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead. Then comes the line: “…in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.” Notice those words, 'in a sense.' I'll keep them right where the writer put them.

The text says the opposite, friend. Hebrews 11:19 says “…in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.” Those words 'in a sense' matter, so don't skip over them. Abraham had reasoned that God could raise the dead.

He worships. Jacob blessed each of Joseph's sons and worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff. He's dying, he's leaning on a staff, and he's still worshiping. I can barely get through a morning without leaning on the counter and complaining.

Weeping isn't in this verse, friend. It says Jacob worshiped as he leaned on the top of his staff. That's right after he blessed each of Joseph's sons. If you want tears, I'll supply them, because I get misty over a perfectly stamped cookie.

Esau shows up in verse 20, when Isaac blesses Jacob and Esau. He isn't in verse 21, though. There, Jacob blesses each of Joseph's sons and worships as he leans on the top of his staff. Different verse, different scene, friend.

That's it, friend. With his end near, Joseph spoke about the exodus of the Israelites. Most of us use our last words to ask where the good oven mitts went. This man is looking at the whole future of a people.
That's not what this verse says. Hebrews 11:22 says Joseph spoke about the exodus of the Israelites. He also gave instructions about his bones. Keep your eyes on the exodus, friend.

explanations.answer: A new king rising in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Close to the neighborhood but not the house, friend. Hebrews 11:22 says Joseph spoke about the exodus of the Israelites. It names no new king. The verse is looking ahead to Israel leaving.

It's the other way around, friend. The writer says Moses' parents hid him for three months, and “…they were unafraid of the king’s edict.” They saw that he was a beautiful child. Staying unafraid of a king's edict is more nerve than I have on a Monday.
False. The text says “…they were unafraid of the king’s edict.” By faith they hid Moses for three months after his birth. They saw that he was a beautiful child.

Hebrews 11:25 says the reverse, friend. It says Moses “…chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin.” So he picked suffering with God's people. He took the hard seat over the comfy one that doesn't last.

False. The text says Moses “…chose to suffer oppression with God’s people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin.” So he went with God's people, not with the enjoyment. That word 'fleeting' says it all, friend. He picked the hard seat with God's people over the comfy one that doesn't last.
Reward, friend. The writer says Moses valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt “…for he was looking ahead to his reward.” He wasn't just gritting his teeth. He was looking ahead.

A throne, friend? Nice guess, but nobody's handing out thrones in this verse. It says Moses valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt, “…for he was looking ahead to his reward.” Reward is the word, and I'd hold onto it tighter than the last cookie in the box.

A palace? That's a lot of house to guess, friend. The verse sets disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt and never mentions a palace. What Moses was looking ahead to is his reward, and that's the word the writer picked.

explanations.answer: He saw the God no one can see
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The writer says Moses “…persevered because he saw Him who is invisible.” That's what carried him when he left Egypt, not fearing the king's anger. Keep that line close, friend.

explanations.answer: He had his brother Aaron beside him
explanations.explanation: Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), is a fine fellow, but he isn't named in this verse. The writer says Moses persevered because he saw Him who is invisible. That's what kept him going, friend.

explanations.answer: He heard the people cheering him on
explanations.explanation: No cheering section in this verse, friend. The writer says Moses “…persevered because he saw Him who is invisible.” That's what the writer points to, not a crowd.

True, friend. By faith Moses kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, “…so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel’s own firstborn.” The writer puts those two things right next to that result. That's the whole point of the verse.

The text says the other way, friend. Moses kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood “…so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel’s own firstborn.” That's the reason the writer gives. So this one is true.

Dry, friend. The writer says by faith the people passed through the Red Sea “…as on dry land…” Think about that: a whole sea, and they crossed it as on dry land. That's a sentence worth reading twice.
Mud would be a rough walk, friend, but that's not what the writer says. He says the people passed through the Red Sea “…as on dry land…” No mud in this verse. The picture he gives is dry land.
Rocks aren't in this verse, friend. The writer says the people passed through the Red Sea “…as on dry land…” That word 'dry' is the one to hold onto. They crossed by faith.

It went differently, friend. The writer says that when the Egyptians tried to follow, “…they were drowned.” The people of Israel crossed by faith, but the Egyptians did not make it. That's a heavy end to the verse, so I'll just say it plainly.

False. By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as on dry land, “but when the Egyptians tried to follow, they were drowned.” The Egyptians did not make it across. That's a heavy line, and the writer states it plainly.

They marched around them. The walls of Jericho fell by faith, “…after the people had marched around them for seven days.” No battering ram in the verse, friend. Just a lot of walking and a lot of faith.

Nobody grabbed a shovel in this verse, friend. The writer says the walls of Jericho fell “…after the people had marched around them for seven days.” Marching is the action he names. That's what the people did.

No arrows in this verse, friend. The text says the walls of Jericho fell “…after the people had marched around them for seven days.” It's all marching, day after day. That's the part the writer points to.

She welcomed them in peace. Rahab, the prostitute, is on this list because by faith she did not perish with those who were disobedient. The writer says that was “…because she welcomed the spies in peace…” Notice who's on the list, friend. It's a bigger table than you'd guess.

explanations.answer: She reported them to the king
explanations.explanation: That's not what the writer says, friend. He says Rahab, the prostitute, did not perish with those who were disobedient “…because she welcomed the spies in peace…” Welcoming is her action here. No report to the king in this verse.

explanations.answer: She kept them out of the city
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The writer says Rahab, the prostitute, “…welcomed the spies in peace…” That's why she did not perish with those who were disobedient.

Time, friend. The writer says, “Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon…” and keeps going down the list. He's got more names than he's got room. I know the feeling, because I've run out of rack space for cookies more than once.
Custom isn't in this verse, friend. The writer says “Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon…” and then rattles off more names. It's about running out of time, not about how things are done.
Modesty isn't what holds him back, friend. The writer says, “Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon…” He's got a long list and a short stretch of time to fit it in. The word he uses is time.

explanations.answer: They shut the mouths of lions
explanations.explanation: They shut the mouths of lions, friend. The writer lists it right alongside conquering kingdoms and administering justice. And all of it is through faith.

explanations.answer: They chased lions out of the land
explanations.explanation: Chasing isn't in this verse, friend. It says these people of faith “…shut the mouths of lions…” Shutting mouths is the action the writer names, not chasing.

explanations.answer: They hunted lions for the king
explanations.explanation: No hunting trip in this verse, friend. The writer says they “…shut the mouths of lions…” That's what faith did here. No king is mentioned in connection with it.
Fire, friend. The verse says they “…quenched the raging fire…” Then it adds that they escaped the edge of the sword. I get nervous when my oven runs a little hot, so I'm tipping my hat to them.
Flood isn't in this verse, friend. It says they “…quenched the raging fire…” and escaped the edge of the sword. The word here is fire.
A storm? Nice try, friend. The writer says they “…quenched the raging fire…” and escaped the edge of the sword. A storm would blow right past a bakery, but fire I take personally.

True, friend. The writer says these people of faith “…gained strength from weakness…” That line sits right between escaping the edge of the sword and becoming mighty in battle. Honestly, that gives me some hope.

The text says it's true, friend. The writer says these people of faith “…gained strength from weakness…” It's right there in verse 34, next to becoming mighty in battle. Weakness wasn't the end of the story for them.

explanations.answer: So they might gain a better resurrection
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the writer gives. Others were tortured and refused their release “…so that they might gain a better resurrection.” I think this is one of the heaviest parts of the whole chapter. So I'll slow down here, friend, and just say it plainly.

explanations.answer: So their families would be spared
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason, friend. These people refused their release “…so that they might gain a better resurrection.” Families aren't mentioned in the verse. I think it's a heavy verse, so I'm sticking to just what it says.

explanations.answer: So the king would change his mind
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't say that, friend. He says they refused their release “…so that they might gain a better resurrection.” No king is named in this verse. I think this is a heavy one, so I'll stay with the exact words.
The writer flips it, friend. He says, “The world was not worthy of them.” So the statement has it backwards. This comes right after the swords, the deserts and the caves and holes in the ground.

False, and the flip matters. The writer says, “The world was not worthy of them.” They wandered in deserts and mountains, and hid in caves and holes in the ground. Even so, the writer says it is the world that fell short of them.

Something better for us. Hebrews 11:40 says, “God had planned something better for us…” After that long list of faith, that line lands like the smell of fresh cookies coming out of the oven. It means we're part of it, friend.
That's not what the writer says, friend. He says, “God had planned something better for us…” A new test isn't mentioned in this verse. Better is the word.
No new list in this verse, friend. The writer says, “God had planned something better for us…” After all those names, he turns to what God had planned. That word 'better' is the one to keep.

True, friend. The writer says God planned something better for us, “…so that together with us they would be made perfect.” Together is the word. All those names on the list, and us too, in the same line.
The text says otherwise, friend. God had planned something better for us, “…so that together with us they would be made perfect.” So they aren't left out. They're made perfect together with us.
